summary: Extends DHCPv6 Leasequery, which could only ask about one binding at a time, with new query types and bulk transfer of binding data over TCP. This is a Proposed Standard, later updated by RFC 7653.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of asking a landlord about one apartment at a time, you can ask for the whole list in one go.

questions: how to get many dhcpv6 lease records at once
how does bulk leasequery differ from leasequery
which tcp port does bulk leasequery use
what is the dhcpv6 relay-id option
subtitle: How a DHCPv6 relay can pull whole sets of lease and prefix bindings from a server over TCP.

tldr.problem: DHCPv6 Leasequery can only ask about one binding at a time, and only when the requestor already knows which binding it wants. A relay that has rebooted and lost its routes for delegated prefixes cannot work that way.
tldr.mechanism: Bulk Leasequery opens a TCP connection to the server on port 547, sends a LEASEQUERY with one of three new query types (by relay ID, link address or Remote-ID), and gets back a stream of LEASEQUERY-REPLY, LEASEQUERY-DATA and LEASEQUERY-DONE messages.
tldr.outcome: A relay can recover thousands of bindings in one exchange. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 7653.

today: RFC 5460 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it was later updated by RFC 7653, so read the two together.

sections.title: Why Single Queries Are Not Enough
sections.content:
A DHCPv6 server keeps the authoritative record of which addresses and delegated prefixes (bindings) it has handed out. In a service-provider network, the edge router often acts as a DHCPv6 relay agent and is also responsible for keeping routes to the prefixes delegated to clients. If that router is replaced or reboots, it needs to get the binding data back from the server so that the prefixes are routable again.

The existing Leasequery protocol (RFC 5007) answers questions about individual bindings. That only works when the requestor already knows the target binding, for example because traffic just arrived. With prefix delegation, the data may be needed before any traffic arrives, so the relay cannot form the individual queries.

RFC 5460 extends Leasequery with new query types and bulk transfer over TCP. It notes that an edge may have many thousands of delegated prefixes per relay, which is why TCP is used.
sections.plainLanguage: A router that forgot who lives where cannot ask about each house by name, because it forgot the names. This memo lets it say 'tell me about every house I look after.'

sections.title: How a Bulk Leasequery Works
sections.content:
The design is modelled on the individual Leasequery protocol; most differences come from using TCP. The client opens a TCP connection to the server on DHCPv6 port 547, so it needs the server's address from configuration or some other means, and unicast reachability. No relaying is specified for bulk leasequery.

The client sends a LEASEQUERY carrying a query type and data about the bindings it wants. The server replies with a LEASEQUERY-REPLY that says whether the query succeeded and, if it did, includes the first client's binding data. Further clients' bindings follow in LEASEQUERY-DATA messages. If the server sent at least one client's bindings, it ends with a LEASEQUERY-DONE.

The client may reuse the connection for more queries, and either end can close it once all data has been sent. Only these four message types are allowed on the connection, and it is not an alternative way for clients to get DHCPv6 service.

The new query types cannot be used with UDP Leasequery. Servers that implement both MUST NOT accept them in UDP messages and MUST answer with the NotAllowed status code. The Client Link option from RFC 5007 MUST NOT appear in bulk replies.
sections.plainLanguage: You phone the office and ask your question. They answer the first part, read out the rest of the list one item at a time, then say 'that is everything.'

sections.title: TCP Framing and the New Messages
sections.content:
TCP is a byte stream, so the receiver needs to know where each DHCPv6 message ends. Two octets holding the message size in network byte order are put in front of each DHCPv6 message sent on a Bulk Leasequery connection. This framing is not compatible with the UDP message format: a TCP-framed request sent over UDP may be invalid because the fields are offset by the size prefix.

Two message types are new. LEASEQUERY-DATA carries data about a single client's leases and prefix bindings on a single link, to reduce redundant data. It MUST be preceded by a LEASEQUERY-REPLY, MUST be sent only in answer to a successful query, and only when more than one client's data is returned. Its transaction-id MUST match the request, and the Server-ID, Client-ID and status code options SHOULD NOT be included.

LEASEQUERY-DONE marks the end of a group of replies. A single one MUST be sent after all replies to a successful request that returned at least one binding. If the server hits an error after it has already sent the first reply, it SHOULD try to send a LEASEQUERY-DONE with a status code option describing the error.
sections.plainLanguage: Each letter gets a note on the front saying how long it is, so the reader knows where one letter stops and the next starts.

sections.title: New Query Types and the Relay-ID Option
sections.content:
Three query types are added, all aimed at helping a relay recover data it has lost:

  • QUERY_BY_RELAY_ID: returns bindings tied to a relay's DUID. If the link-address field is 0::0, it asks for all bindings for that relay; otherwise only bindings on that link.
  • QUERY_BY_LINK_ADDRESS: returns bindings on the network segment identified by a link-address a relay may have used in a Relay-Forward message.
  • QUERY_BY_REMOTE_ID: returns bindings tied to a Relay Agent Remote-ID option value (RFC 4649). The server must have recorded the most recent Remote-ID with its binding data.

To support the first, the RFC defines the Relay-ID option (OPTION_RELAY_ID), which carries a DUID identifying the relay. A relay MAY include it in Relay-Forward messages, and a server MAY associate it with the resulting bindings. Without the option, a server cannot answer QUERY_BY_RELAY_ID. A relay SHOULD generate a DUID, keep it in stable storage, and let it be configured, so an administrator can replace a relay and keep the link to existing bindings.

One new status code, QueryTerminated, tells the requestor that the server cannot perform the query or ended it early, for example when short of resources or shutting down. The requestor may retry later after a short wait.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask 'show me everything for this router,' 'everything on this street,' or 'everything with this label on it.'

sections.title: Requestor and Server Behavior
sections.content:
A requestor sends a standard Leasequery from RFC 5007, framed as above. A reply with no OPTION_CLIENT_DATA option means the server had no matching bindings. The reply is complete when that reply arrives (no client data), when LEASEQUERY-DONE arrives (client data was present), or otherwise when the connection closes. A LEASEQUERY-DATA message without client data MUST be discarded, and a LEASEQUERY-DONE for an unknown transaction-id means the client MUST close the connection.

One connection may carry several queries, each with a unique transaction-id. A server MAY interleave replies to parallel queries, so a client that cannot handle interleaving MUST NOT send more than one query at a time. A server MUST NOT read more queries from a connection than it can process at once.

Servers MUST be able to limit active connections, with a default of BULK_LQ_MAX_CONNS (10). They MAY restrict which clients and query types are allowed, and SHOULD close connections from unpermitted clients immediately. Both sides SHOULD be ready to drop a blocked connection after BULK_LQ_DATA_TIMEOUT (300 s), and timeouts smaller than the defaults are NOT RECOMMENDED. If the server finds nothing, it SHOULD send a LEASEQUERY-REPLY with neither a status code nor client data. For relay-ID and Remote-ID queries with a non-zero link-address that matches no link, it SHOULD return NotConfigured.
sections.plainLanguage: The asker waits for 'that is everything' and gives up if the line goes quiet for too long. The answerer only lets a few callers on the line at once.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to the threats already described for DHCPv6 and for Leasequery in RFC 5007, including relayed LEASEQUERY messages, packet-flooding denial of service, restriction to trusted clients and use of IPsec.

Using TCP adds new concerns. Attacks such as SYN flooding can use up the server's connection resources. So can malicious clients that connect and then send invalid queries, partial queries or nothing at all. The RFC recommends that servers let operators limit the sources of incoming connections, limit accepted connections and in-process queries per connection, and limit how long an idle connection stays open.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could tie up all the phone lines and never talk. So the office limits who may call, how many lines are open, and how long a silent line may stay on.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA assigned new values in the DHCPv6 registries for the option, the status code, two message types and the three query types. Option code 53 is OPTION_RELAY_ID, and status code 11 is QueryTerminated. The message types are 16 for LEASEQUERY-DONE and 17 for LEASEQUERY-DATA.
sections.plainLanguage: The new words in this memo were added to the official dictionary with their own numbers.
